plants.name: Camellia japonica
plants.description: An evergreen shrub with glossy dark green leaves and rose-like flowers. It is a favorite winter-blooming ornamental in mild climates, with thousands of cultivars ranging from single to fully double forms.
plants.bloomingSeason: Late autumn to early spring (peak in winter)
plants.location: Native to Japan, Korea, and China; widely cultivated in the southeastern United States, Mediterranean Europe, and Australia
plants.funFact: Camellia sinensis, a close relative, produces the leaves used to make all true tea.

plants.name: Helleborus niger
plants.description: A low-growing perennial with nodding, cup-shaped white flowers with golden stamens that often fade to pink. It blooms in the cold of winter, sometimes pushing up through snow.
plants.location: Native to the mountains of central and southern Europe; grown in temperate gardens worldwide
plants.funFact: Despite its name it is not a rose; all parts of the plant are toxic, and it was historically used in folk medicine and associated with legends of Christmas.

plants.name: Protea cynaroides
plants.description: A striking shrub with giant flower heads made of colorful bracts surrounding a central cone of tiny flowers. In the Southern Hemisphere summer it is among the showiest of the fynbos plants.
plants.bloomingSeason: Late spring to summer in the Southern Hemisphere (Dec–Feb in many areas)
plants.location: South Africa's Western and Eastern Cape fynbos; cultivated in Australia, Hawaii, and California
plants.funFact: It is the national flower of South Africa and can have flower heads up to 30 cm across.

plants.name: Hamamelis mollis
plants.description: A deciduous shrub that bears spidery, fragrant, ribbon-like petals on bare branches in winter. The scented flowers tolerate frost by curling up in severe cold and unfurling again when it warms.
plants.location: Native to central and eastern China; grown in temperate gardens of Europe and North America
plants.funFact: Its flowers can curl up their petals to protect themselves during freezing weather and open again once temperatures rise.
